title: EIA Forecasts 600K BPD Shut-In Through 2027; Houthi Attack Kills Four in Bab el-Mandeb; US Fires on Blockade-Breaking Ship
subhead: The US EIA warned that Middle East oil disruptions will persist into 2027 even if trade normalizes, as Iran's new security chief ruled out reopening Hormuz and dual shipping attacks in the Gulf of Oman and Bab el-Mandeb killed crew members for the first time in the conflict.

sections.heading: EIA: 600,000 BPD to Stay Shut-In Through End of 2027
sections.body:
The US Energy Information Administration released its August Short-Term Energy Outlook on Tuesday, projecting that roughly 600,000 barrels per day of Middle East oil production will remain shut-in through the end of 2027, even under the assumption that trade patterns begin normalizing by early next year. The EIA estimated that 5.5 million bpd of Middle East output — over 5% of global consumption — was offline during July.

The agency now expects global oil output to average 100.8 million bpd in 2026, about 1% below its July forecast, while world demand remains at 104 million bpd. The widening supply deficit prompted the EIA to raise its 2026 Brent price forecast to $86.81/barrel (up from under $82) and WTI to $80.88/barrel (up from just over $76). For 2027, Brent is now projected at $69.39 — a softer decline than previously forecast, reflecting the longer tail of disruptions.

The EIA has previously issued forecasts of an imminent recovery in Hormuz shipments that failed to materialize. This time, the agency was more cautious: it assumes flows through the strait remain severely constrained through August and only begin to slowly increase in September, but acknowledges the uncertainty.
sections.whyItMatters: The EIA's forecast is the most authoritative signal yet that the Iran war's energy impact will not be a short disruption. The 600,000 bpd residual shut-in through 2027 means the market faces a persistent supply deficit even after any peace deal — and the agency's track record of premature optimism suggests even this forecast could prove optimistic.

sections.heading: Houthi Attack in Bab el-Mandeb Kills Four Crew Members
sections.body:
A suspected Houthi attack on the Egyptian-owned cargo vessel Tihamah in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait killed four crew members on Tuesday, Yemen's Transport Ministry said — the first confirmed fatalities from attacks on shipping since the Iran war began. Two Yemeni coast guard rescuers from an anti-Houthi military group were also killed.

The Houthi-run Saba news agency separately claimed responsibility for an attack on a Saudi ship carrying military equipment in the same strait. There was no immediate Saudi response. The Houthis declared last month they would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.

Brent crude settled up 1.4% at $88.91/barrel, while WTI rose 1.3% to $83.20 — both at one-week highs for a second consecutive session, after a 5% jump on Monday when deal hopes faded.
sections.whyItMatters: The first deaths from Houthi attacks on shipping mark a dangerous escalation. Until now, the Red Sea campaign had disrupted trade and raised costs but caused no confirmed crew fatalities. Deaths change the risk calculus for ship owners and insurers, making it harder to convince crews to transit Bab el-Mandeb even if the strait technically remains open.

sections.heading: US Navy Strikes Ship Breaking Iran Blockade in Gulf of Oman
sections.body:
A US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged cargo ship M/V Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman on Tuesday, disabling its steering gear after the crew ignored repeated warnings about violating Washington's naval blockade on Iranian ports, US Central Command said. Maritime sources told Reuters the vessel was hit off Pakistan while sailing into the Gulf of Oman. No casualties were reported.

This is the third reported US action against a vessel since the blockade was reinstated in July. The strike demonstrates that the US is enforcing its Iran blockade with live fire, adding another layer of risk to an already constricted shipping environment in the region.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is willing to use lethal force to enforce its blockade — not just interdict but disable vessels. This raises the stakes for any ship operator considering transit near Iranian waters and further chills commercial traffic in the Gulf of Oman, compounding the Hormuz choke.

sections.heading: Libya Warns of Force Majeure After Drone Attacks on Zawiya
sections.body:
Libya's National Oil Corporation said it could declare force majeure and shut down the Zawiya refinery — the country's largest operating refinery, with a capacity of 120,000 bpd — if drone attacks on its facilities continue. Three drone strikes hit Zawiya over Sunday and Monday, including one that caused an explosion inside a fuel storage tank with visible flames and dense smoke.

The Zawiya complex is linked to Libya's Sharara oilfield, which has a production capacity of 300,000 bpd. NOC said emergency teams brought all fires under control, but warned of a complete shutdown if attacks persist. No group has claimed responsibility for the strikes.

The violence is part of broader instability in the strategic city of Zawiya, approximately 40 km west of Tripoli. Libya, an OPEC member, has been a marginal producer in global terms, but a force majeure declaration would tighten an already strained market.
sections.whyItMatters: A force majeure at Zawiya could knock 120,000 bpd of refining and potentially curtail the 300,000 bpd Sharara field. In a market with 5.5 million bpd already shut-in, every barrel counts — and Libya's instability shows how the Iran war's disruption is cascading into other producer countries dealing with their own conflicts.

sections.heading: Rezaei Draws Hard Line on Hormuz; Naqvi Makes Sixth Mediation Trip to Tehran
sections.body:
Iran's newly appointed Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei declared on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed unless the US ends the war and blockade, releases frozen Iranian assets, and agrees to a wider ceasefire covering Lebanon and Gaza. The conditions go beyond what Iran had previously demanded and mark the strongest indication yet that Hormuz will not reopen quickly.

The statement came as Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi arrived in Tehran for his sixth visit since the conflict began, meeting Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Pakistan, alongside Qatar, has been mediating between the US and Iran, and both countries had earlier suggested the two sides were close to 'some sort' of arrangement. But Naqvi's repeated trips without a breakthrough underscore the gap between the parties.

Trump, for his part, told reporters that the US 'totally controls' the Strait of Hormuz and said of Iran: 'At some point, maybe they'll do something and then they get blown away.' He previously demanded that Iran pay compensation for Americans killed over 50 years of attacks — a demand Tehran dismissed.

Gulf stock markets fell on Tuesday as optimism over a deal faded, Reuters reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Rezaei's appointment and hardline conditions signal that Iran is not softening its posture — if anything, it's expanding its demands to include Lebanon and Gaza. With both sides demanding compensation from each other, the gap between a deal and reality is widening, not narrowing. Meanwhile, Hormuz traffic has dropped from 125-140 vessels per day pre-war to just six on Monday.

sections.heading: India's Russian Oil Share Hits Record 48% as Senate Tariff Bill Looms
sections.body:
Russia's share of India's crude oil imports reached an all-time high of 48% in June 2026, meaning nearly one in every two barrels of crude imported by India came from Russia — despite the US Senate passing legislation that could allow tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas.

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro faced online backlash from Indian commentators but said that Trump and Modi have a 'very good working relationship' and would 'work it out.' The US sanctions waiver on Russian crude has expired, and the Lindsey Graham-authored Senate bill targets the top five countries buying Russian crude, including India and China.

Meanwhile, India's US crude imports are heading for their lowest level since December 2024 at approximately 75,000 bpd in August — down from a peak of 565,000 bpd in October 2025. India sources crude from 41 countries and LNG from 15, but replacing Russian volumes would raise import costs and pressure the rupee.

A bipartisan group of US lawmakers has also introduced a Russia sanctions bill in the House of Representatives, according to Interfax-Ukraine.
sections.whyItMatters: India is voting with its tankers, not its diplomacy — 48% Russian crude is a deliberate bet that the tariff threat won't be enforced. If the Senate bill becomes law and Trump actually imposes 100% tariffs, India faces a brutal choice between energy security and trade access to the US market. Until then, Indian refiners are buying Russian crude at a discount while they still can.

sections.heading: China's Coal-to-Gas Push Aims to Triple Capacity by 2030
sections.body:
Rystad Energy analysis published Monday shows China's coal-to-gas (CTG) industry is set to nearly triple capacity from 9.4 Bcm in 2026 to 28 Bcm by 2030 — making it the world's only large-scale synthetic gas program. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) formalizes CTG as a strategic supply buffer.

Xinjiang province dominates CTG expansion thanks to mine-mouth coal at $30/tonne, less than 40% of Inner Mongolia prices. Delivered gas reaches East China at $9.1-$9.6/MMBtu, generally below China's average LNG import price. Existing plants are running at over 90% utilization, and approximately 20 Bcm/year of capacity is under development. Project approval timelines in Xinjiang have compressed from three years to under 12 months.

Rystad warned that LNG exporters from Australia, Qatar, and the US 'need to model coal-to-gas as a structural dampener on China's import demand, not a footnote.'
sections.whyItMatters: China is building energy autarky the old-fashioned way — converting coal into gas at mine-mouth prices that undercut LNG imports. If 28 Bcm of CTG comes online by 2030, it could displace roughly 20 million tonnes of annual LNG demand, reshaping the economics of every LNG export project banking on Chinese offtake.

bottomLine: The energy picture darkened on multiple fronts. The EIA's most authoritative assessment yet says 600,000 bpd will stay offline through 2027 — a long-tail disruption even if peace comes. On the water, the first crew deaths from Houthi attacks and the third US enforcement action against a blockade-breaking vessel show that shipping risk is escalating, not normalizing. Iran's new security chief expanded Hormuz conditions to include Lebanon and Gaza, while Pakistan's sixth mediation trip produced no breakthrough. Oil prices continue climbing, with Brent back above $89. Away from Hormuz, Libya's Zawiya refinery faces force majeure from drone attacks, India is doubling down on Russian crude at a record 48% despite tariff threats, and China is building a $9/MMBtu coal-to-gas alternative that could eat 20 million tonnes of future LNG demand. The market is pricing in a disruption that lasts — and the data is starting to confirm it.
sources: Reuters (2), EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook, The Star Malaysia, GMA Network, DevDiscourse, The Media Line, News18, Anadolu Agency, Trak.in, New Indian Express, Rystad Energy via OilPrice.com, Yahoo News, MSN, Financial Express, Interfax-Ukraine
